GC.16.stem: The President can make treaties and appoint officials only 'by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate.' What does this requirement create?

choices.text: a power the President may use only in wartime
a rule that the Supreme Court must approve treaties
a legislative check on executive power
a duty for the House to sign each appointment

GC.16.reteach: Reread Article II, Section 2; connect Senate 'Advice and Consent' to checks and balances.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the power is not limited to wartime.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the Senate, not the Court, provides advice and consent.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Prior-knowledge error — the House has no confirmation role over appointments.

GC.16.key_rationale: Requiring Senate advice and consent is a legislative check on the President's treaty and appointment powers.
GC.16.dok_rationale: Requires explaining the effect of the clause, not naming a power.
GC.16.blooms_rationale: Student explains the check created by advice and consent.

GC.18.stem: How can a candidate win the most votes nationwide yet still lose the presidency?

choices.text: Most states give all their electoral votes winner-take-all, so the totals can differ
The Supreme Court picks the President in each election
Congress disregards the popular vote entirely
The Cabinet casts the deciding presidential votes

GC.18.reteach: Reteach the Electoral College math (270 of 538) and winner-take-all; work through a popular/electoral split.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the Court does not choose the President.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the popular vote decides each state's electors.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the Cabinet plays no role in electing the President.

GC.18.key_rationale: Because most states award electors winner-take-all, an electoral-vote majority can differ from the national popular vote.
GC.18.dok_rationale: Requires analyzing how the electoral system can diverge from the popular vote.
GC.18.blooms_rationale: Student analyzes the cause of a popular/electoral split.

formA.stem: Which statement best represents an argument in favor of keeping the Electoral College?

choices.text: It guarantees the national popular-vote winner always takes office
It removes the states from the presidential election entirely
It protects smaller states and pushes candidates to campaign nationally
It lets Congress choose the President in every election

formA.reteach: Reteach the pro/con debate; list supporters' arguments (small-state protection, national campaigns) vs. critics'.

distractor_tags.label: A
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — the popular-vote winner does not always win the Electoral College.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — states are central to the Electoral College.

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Nearby error — the House decides only if no candidate wins a majority, not every election.

formA.key_rationale: A common pro-argument is that the Electoral College protects smaller states and encourages national campaigning.
formA.dok_rationale: Requires evaluating which statement is a valid argument for the system.
formA.blooms_rationale: Student evaluates arguments for the Electoral College.

formB.stem: How is each state's number of Electoral College electors determined?

choices.text: by adding the state's number of senators and representatives
by the size of the state's land area
by giving an equal number to every state
by the number of counties in the state

formB.reteach: Reread Article II, Section 1; compute a state's electors as senators plus representatives.

distractor_tags.label: B
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — land area does not set electoral votes.

distractor_tags.label: C
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — electors are not equal for every state (that is the Senate rule).

distractor_tags.label: D
distractor_tags.rationale: Misconception — counties do not determine electors.

formB.key_rationale: A state's electors equal its number of senators plus its representatives.
formB.dok_rationale: Requires explaining the rule that sets electoral votes, not recalling a number.
formB.blooms_rationale: Student explains how electors are apportioned.
